v.why: With e4 removed, node 3 relies on fewer inputs, so adding the input-to-output skip restores a much-needed residual path and gains more (exps 15-17 vs 11-14).
In parameter-poor pooling cells an extra identity path to the output dilutes the already weak features and hurts accuracy (exp 19), unlike conv cells where it helps.
Removing the e3 skip when e4 is also absent removes most or all paths into the output node, causing much larger drops (exps 65, 67).
If e5 is already none, deleting e4 leaves the output fed only by e3 (or nothing), so the loss is far larger (exps 33, 34).
Without the e3 skip, e4 is a key output path and its removal hurts more (exps 32, 34 vs 31).
Adding a conv on a previously missing edge into the output gives more benefit than swapping an existing op (exps 92, 95, 97, 98 vs 91, 93, 94).
Replacing a 1x1 conv with a 3x3 conv on e5 gives little or negative gain, while replacing none, skip, or pool gives clear gains (exp 3 vs 1, 2, 4).
When there is no direct input-to-output skip, a skip on e0 supplies a residual route through node 1, offsetting the conv loss (exp 87 vs 81-86).
With e0 absent, e1 is the only route from the input into the deeper nodes, so replacing its conv with pooling is much more damaging (exp 49).
When e2 is none, node 1 feeds only e4, so strengthening e0 benefits fewer downstream paths and the gain shrinks (exps 25, 26 vs 21-24).

When node 3 still has other inputs, the same edit moves accuracy by only a few points.

| 9 | e1 → avg_pool_3x3 | e0 = none | lower | Exp 49 |
| 10 | e0 → nor_conv_3x3 | e2 = none | lower | Exps 25, 26 vs. 21–24 |
